cells.tense: You are here at the bench, and the practice is carrying itself now.
cells.ask: Choose one small thing you already do well and repeat it at a fixed time tomorrow, then stop when the time is up.
cells.core: You're at the bench and the work is carrying itself. The repetition became something you do rather than something you force, and the aloneness of it isn't a wall — it's the condition that lets the skill settle into your hands. You can feel when to add a little and when to leave it alone, and that sensing is making small adjustments all through the session.\n\nThe refining isn't feeding worry; it's feeding growth. When something false falls away, it falls because you've practiced enough to recognize what doesn't hold. Keep the small light lit. The ask is to pick one thing you already do well, repeat it at a fixed time tomorrow, and stop when the time is up — letting the completion be the point, not the next thing.

cells.tense: You will keep refining until the work is beyond reproach, and the future you're bracing for doesn't arrive.
cells.ask: Finish one practice session today at the point it's good enough, then close the notebook and walk away for the rest of the evening.
cells.core: You're refining ahead of yourself. Somewhere in front of you is a version where the work is finally clean enough, and you're living in that version — so every session becomes a repair, and stopping feels like losing ground. The isolation that used to be chosen now feels required. You're not practicing anymore; you're guarding.\n\nThe fear is that if you stop, something falls apart. But the practice was not the thing holding it together. The ask is to finish one session today the moment it's good enough, close the notebook, and leave it for the evening. Not because the work is done — because you are.

cells.tense: You are not practicing, and you have not been for a while.
cells.ask: Put twenty minutes on a timer today for one small thing you used to be good at, and let the timer end it whether or not it felt right.
cells.core: The practice isn't running. There's a thing you could be doing daily, something small and repetitive, and it isn't in your days. When you think about starting, the thought slides off — not frightening, just weightless. Keeping something going is what's thin here, not the want.\n\nWhat's needed isn't more willpower. It's a small, fair exchange: twenty minutes on a timer today for one thing you used to be good at, with the timer ending it whether or not it felt right. That's it. Not a return to anything. A single fair turn, and the timer carries the stop so you don't have to.

cells.tense: You are already practicing, and you talk about it as if it were happening to you.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're already good at and say out loud, once, that you got there by doing it — then keep going.
cells.core: You're already practicing. The way you handle your work, the thing people comment on, the ease that looks like no effort — the repetition happened, but you describe it as just how you are. The doing happened. You didn't say so. You've been saying 'I'm not really trying' or 'anyone could do this,' and that story costs you credit for something you made.\n\nThere's a difference between modesty and erasing yourself from the account. You don't need to announce it to anyone. You just need to stop pretending the skill fell on you. The ask is to pick one thing you're already good at, say out loud once that you got there by doing it, and then keep going.

attempts.check: The record gives no history for the Too Little card, so I avoid claiming what made practice feel dangerous; the reader may object that they never had an early bad experience with practice, only a long drift — the cell should land as withdrawal from practice, not as a single past wound. The ask survives a wrong read because anyone can choose one small thing to set down at a fixed time; it does not require knowing why cultivation stalled. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person would be any line that praises the reader for having 'quiet wisdom' they haven't claimed — cut that.
